studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops writing an in-depth description of an event independently within the unit “In-Depth Study: Character, Setting, Event, and Point of View.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's independent application a work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
From the hallway outside Studio B, the power flicker on that Thursday in March lasted long enough for the emergency light above the fire door to click on and then off again.

The station manager, Desmond Ruiz, was walking toward the front office when it happened. He stopped, counted to five, and turned around.

He had been a broadcast engineer for nineteen years, and he already knew three things that the two people inside Studio B did not yet know. He knew the automation server did not write its playlist to disk until the top of the hour. He knew that meant roughly fifty minutes of programming had just ceased to exist as a record. And he knew the station's sponsor contracts required a verified log.

He reached the studio door and stopped with his hand on the handle, because through the glass he could see Ramona Fitch standing over the board with both hands pressed flat on it, and beside her the spring intern, holding up a clipboard.

Desmond watched for a moment. Then he took his hand off the handle and walked back to the front office.

His assistant asked him whether everything was all right in there.

"They have it," he said.

"You are sure?"

Desmond sat down. He thought about the nineteen years, and about how many times he had walked into a room to fix something that was already being fixed, and how long it had taken him to learn that walking in has a cost.

"The kid kept a paper log," he said. "Nobody told her to keep it that carefully. She just did."

He signed the incident report at four fifteen and wrote one sentence in the notes field: *No loss. Manual record maintained.*

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “The Same Thursday, Told from the Hallway”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what writing an in-depth description of an event independently asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “The Same Thursday, Told from the Hallway,” then answer: Independently annotate the reading for writing an in-depth description of an event independently. Which annotation leads to the strongest inference?

Deliverable: Grade 4: an annotated reading plus a supported inference; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If writing an in-depth description of an event independently is not yet secure, return to “The Same Thursday, Told from the Hallway” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply writing an in-depth description of an event independently to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “The Same Thursday, Told from the Hallway.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
